_README: config_opdiff_dense.json -- the DENSE REFERENCE for the opdiff task, and
the configuration the learnability calibration (T-OD.10) is run with.
WHAT IT IS. The same engine, the same data, the same loss -- and a plain
one-block transformer: `max_depth = 1` with the MoR architecture means one
shared FFN (width 28) per token, no routing and no recursion. It is the
reference the study's claims are read against, and it answers a question
the three arms cannot: WHEN IS AN OPERATION LEARNABLE AT ALL?
WHY IT IS NEEDED, and what it decides. The first full-scale run showed that
the F rows are at chance for EVERY k -- including k = 1, the easiest one --
while the other six groups reach 0.85 per-digit accuracy. That is a fact
about the DATA (one F iteration is a 32x32-bit modular multiplication,
which a 4 M-parameter transformer cannot learn without chain of thought),
not about the architecture. A dense reference says the same thing without
any mixture or recursion in the picture, and its per-k curve is the
frontier: the largest k at which a plain model still learns the operation.
The F operation is then redesigned against that frontier rather than
guessed at.
IT IS A REFERENCE, NOT A MATRIX CELL. The run name says so --
`opdiffB_dense_MoR_seed42` -- and the aggregator's matrix pattern cannot
match it, so a dense reference can never be admitted to the three-arm
table. It is reported beside the arms, in its own row, labelled.
